product.title: Irish 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take Irish (Gaeilge) from zero to A1: short dialogues set in a house in Galway, word-for-word translations that take every word apart, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Irish is the first official language of the Republic of Ireland and one of the oldest written languages in Western Europe — and it works in a genuinely different way from English: the verb comes first in the sentence, there are no words for "yes" and "no", there is no verb "to have", and the first letter of a word can change depending on the word in front of it. This course takes it all slowly, one small table per unit, always through whole sentences you can use straight away.

blocks.text: Irish — *Gaeilge* in its own name — is the first official language of the Republic of Ireland, an official language of the European Union, and the oldest written language in Western Europe after Latin and Greek. Its oldest texts are fifteen hundred years old. It isn't English with an accent, and it isn't a dialect: it's a completely different branch of the Indo-European tree, a close cousin of Scottish Gaelic and Manx and a distant one of Welsh and Breton.

That sounds remote. But you've met Irish more often than you think. *Whiskey* comes from *uisce beatha*, "water of life". *Slogan* comes from *slua-ghairm*, "battle cry of the host" — by way of Scottish Gaelic. *Galore* comes from *go leor*, "enough". Names you hear every day — Kevin, Brian, Kennedy, Brennan, Donovan, Siobhán, Niamh — are all Irish words frozen into names.
Three things about the language are genuinely new, and it's better to know all three now than to be surprised halfway through.

**First: the verb comes first.** Not "I drink tea" but "Drink-I tea" — *Ólaim tae*. Not "Budi is at home" but "Is Budi at home" — *Tá Budi sa bhaile*. The order is verb–subject–object, and once your ear gets used to it, it's actually very predictable: the first word almost always tells you what's happening.

**Second: there are no words for "yes" and "no".** Really none. If someone asks *An bhfuil tú go maith?* ("Are you well?"), you don't answer "yes"; you repeat the verb: *Tá* ("am") or *Níl* ("am not"). Asked *Ar ól tú tae?* ("Did you drink tea?"), you answer *D'ól* or *Níor ól*. The habit runs so deep that Irish people carry it into English: "Did you see him?" — "I did, yeah."

**Third: the first letter of a word can change.** *Carr* ("car") becomes *mo charr* ("my car") and *ár gcarr* ("our car"). The first letter isn't replaced; it's **softened** (an *h* slips in — this is called *séimhiú*) or **covered** (another letter goes in front — this is called *urú*). This is what sends beginners astray in the dictionary most often, so this course marks every change from the very first unit and gathers all the rules together in Unit 19.

Once you're past those three, a lot of Irish feels surprisingly light. Nouns don't change through as many cases as in German or Russian. There's no verb "to have" to learn — possession is simply "there is … at me". And feelings sit *on* a person: *Tá ocras orm* — "there is hunger on me". You can still hear these patterns in Irish English: "the hunger is on me", "I'm after eating".

According to the 2022 census, about twenty thousand people speak it daily in the *Gaeltacht* — the pockets of native speakers in Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Kerry, Cork, Waterford, and Meath — and about seventy thousand across all of Ireland, while more than one and a half million others say they can use it. This course uses *An Caighdeán Oifigiúil*, the standard form used in schools, law, and broadcasting; the pronunciation follows the Connacht (Galway) dialect, which sits in the middle between Munster in the south and Ulster in the north. Where the difference is big, the course says so.

The twenty units ahead are meant to be worked through one at a time, about three or four days per unit. Don't memorize the tables first; read the dialogue aloud until it feels comfortable in your mouth, then look at the explanation. The language isn't hard — only its spelling needs an introduction, and that introduction is the fourth chapter of this book. *Ádh mór ort!* — good luck.

Every unit has the same structure, and there's a reason for it. You meet the language first as living sentences, and only then the explanation. Reversing that order — memorizing the tables of letter changes first — is the fastest way to make Irish feel impossible.
Set aside thirty to forty minutes a day. Four days in a row of half an hour each beats one whole day once a week; Irish spelling sticks through short, frequent repetition, not long sittings.

items: **By the end of this unit** — three things you'll be able to do once the unit is done. Read them first, and again at the end as a self-check.

**Dialogue** — twelve lines of natural conversation. Each line has three layers: Irish, a natural translation, then a **word-for-word** translation that takes every word apart (`at-me`, `in-the-home`, `drink-I`). That literal layer is the main tool of this course.
**Dialogue notes** — four notes that answer the questions that just popped into your head while reading.
**Grammar sections** — two or three sections, with tables and warning boxes for the mistakes English speakers typically make.
**Vocabulary** — about thirty words from the unit, each with a pronunciation guide spelled for English speakers.
**Exercises** — four sets, twenty-four questions. Do them on paper, not in your head.
**Answer key** — on the following page. Check yourself, and when you're wrong, find the dialogue line that has the pattern.

blocks.title: How to read the word-for-word translation
items: Hyphens join pieces that are fused into a single word in Irish. *Agam* → `at-me`. *Orm* → `on-me`. *Liom* → `with-me`. *Ólaim* → `drink-I`.
Words whose first letter has changed are glossed as they are; the change is explained in the notes, not in the literal layer. *Mo theach* → `my house`.
Irish often puts the verb first, so the literal layer does too: *Tá Máire sa bhaile* → `is Máire in-the-home`.
The literal translation is deliberately awkward. If it read naturally, it would fail to show how Irish builds its sentences.

blocks.title: Why this course prints pronunciation instead of providing audio
items: The voice service used by the Linguo Library doesn't have a single Irish voice yet, so tap-to-listen is deliberately not offered in this course. Voicing Irish with an English speech engine would teach the wrong pronunciation, and that does more harm than silence.

Instead, every vocabulary line and every table has a **Say it** column spelled for English speakers, and Unit 0 — the chapter "Irish pronunciation and spelling" — is longer than in our other language courses.

To hear native speakers, these two free sources are the most useful: *TG4* (the Irish-language TV channel, tg4.ie) and *RTÉ Raidió na Gaeltachta*. The online dictionary *teanglann.ie* has recordings of every word in **three dialects** — listen to the one labeled *Connachta* to match the pronunciation in this course.

blocks.title: If you only have ten minutes today
items: Read the dialogue aloud once, all the way through, without stopping at words you don't know.
Read it once more while following the literal layer.
Close the book. Tomorrow, start from the dialogue notes. Ten minutes actually done beats an hour only planned.

blocks.text: Before Unit 1 begins, it helps to know that this language has already reached you from two directions. Some Irish words crossed into English and from there went around the world; in the other direction, Irish borrowed hundreds of words from Latin and English. The two directions meet in the lists below.
Irish words that went global

Personal names are the same. *Seán* is the Irish form of John; *Caoimhín* (Kevin) is built from *caomh* ("gentle, dear"); *Brian* is usually taken to mean "noble", though its origin is still debated. Surnames beginning with *Ó* mean "grandson of" and *Mac* means "son of" — *Ó Cinnéide* became Kennedy, *Ó Braonáin* became Brennan, *Mac Cárthaigh* became McCarthy.
Old loans from Latin — the same roots English has
Modern words — almost the same in both languages

blocks.title: Two words you'll see every day in Ireland
items: *Fáilte* (FAWL-tyuh) — "welcome". It's written at the entrance to almost every town. The full form is *Céad míle fáilte* — "a hundred thousand welcomes".
*Sláinte* (SLAWN-tyuh) — "health", said when raising a glass. The two words rhyme, and both end in *-te*, read "tyeh", not "tay".

blocks.text: This is the most important chapter in the whole course, and the only one worth reading twice. Irish spelling has a bad reputation that isn't entirely fair: it doesn't look like English, but it is **regular**. Once the six rules below sink in, you'll be able to read words you've never seen correctly — something you can't do even in English. In the **Say it** column throughout this course, capitals mark the stressed syllable. Long vowels: **aw** as in "law", **ay** as in "say" (held, without the glide), **ee** as in "see", **oh** as in "go" (without the glide), **oo** as in "food". Short vowels: **a** as in "cat", **e** as in "bed", **i** as in "bit", **o** as in "hot", **u** as in "but"; at the end of a syllable **ah**, **eh**, **ih**, and **uh** for the weak vowel in "about". **ow** as in "how", **ohw** as in "go" with a light *w*, **ai** as in "Thai". **kh** is the *ch* of Scottish "loch", **gh** is its voiced partner, **sh** as in "ship", **tch** as in "church", and a **y** after a consonant (**ty**, **dy**, **ky**, **gy**, **ly**, **ny** …) is a little *y* glide — the "slender" sound explained in Rule 5.
Rule 1 — Stress falls on the first syllable

Almost always. *Gaeilge* is GAYL-guh, not gay-EL-guh. *Fáilte* is FAWL-tyuh. The most common exceptions: loanwords and words whose long vowel comes later — *cupán* (kuh-PAWN), *arán* (uh-RAWN), *dinnéar* (dih-NYAYR). In the Say it column throughout this course, the syllable **in capitals** is the stressed one. (Munster dialect in the southwest moves the stress to the next syllable when the first is short and a long vowel follows — that's why people in Kerry say ka-LEEN for *cailín* and people in Galway say KAH-leen.)
Rule 2 — The fada lengthens the vowel
The slanted line over a vowel (á é í ó ú) is called the *síneadh fada*, "long stroke". It isn't a stress mark but a **length** mark, and it changes the meaning of a word. Never leave it out.

The five long sounds: **á** like the *aw* in "law" (or a long *a* as in "father"); **é** like the *ay* in "say", held without gliding; **í** like the *ee* in "see"; **ó** like the *o* in "go", held without gliding; **ú** like the *oo* in "food".
Rule 3 — There are only 18 letters

The Irish alphabet has no **j, k, q, v, w, x, y, z**. If you see one of those, the word is an unassimilated loan (*jab*, *x-gha*). Missing k and v doesn't mean the sounds are missing — the "k" sound is written **c** (always hard, never "s"), and the "v" sound is written **bh** or **mh**. That brings us to the next rule.
Rule 4 — An h after a consonant changes its sound (séimhiú)

This is the key to the whole system. In Irish the letter *h* almost never stands on its own; its job is to soften the consonant in front of it. This softening is called **séimhiú** (SHAY-woo), or *lenition*, and it produces the nine pairs below. Learn this table — it's used on every page of the course.

blocks.title: Three traps for English speakers in this table
items: **th is not the English "th" sound.** *Theach* is read "HYAKH", not "theach". Irish has no *th* sound like the one in *think* at all.
**ph isn't "p-h" pronounced separately,** but f — just as in *phone*. And **fh really is silent**: write five letters, read three.

**Broad dh and gh** are roughly a gargled sound at the back of the throat, close to a French *r*. If you can't make it yet, just drop it — native speakers often drop it themselves in the middle of a word.

blocks.text: Rule 5 — Consonants come in two flavors: broad and slender

Every Irish consonant has two forms, and what decides the form is **the vowels on either side of it**. The vowels *a, o, u* make a consonant **broad** (*leathan*); the vowels *e, i* make it **slender** (*caol*). A slender consonant is pronounced as if a small *y* slipped in after it.

head: Letter
Broad (next to a/o/u)
Slender (next to e/i)
rows: thick d, tongue on the teeth — *dán* (DAWN)
thick t, tongue on the teeth — *tá* (TAW)

blocks.text: That's why Irish spelling looks so full of vowels: many written vowels **aren't there to be pronounced** but to tell you whether the consonant next to them is broad or slender. In *sean* ("old"), the *e* isn't pronounced — it only makes the *s* slender, so it reads "SHAN". In *bainne* ("milk"), the *i* makes the *n* slender, and the word reads "BAH-nyuh".

blocks.title: The golden rule of spelling: caol le caol, leathan le leathan
items: "Slender with slender, broad with broad" — the vowels on both sides of a consonant must be the same kind. If there's an *i* or *e* on the left, there must be an *i* or *e* on the right too.
That's why word endings keep changing shape: *ólann* (with a) but *tuigeann* (with e); *fear amháin* but *fir* for the plural.
You don't need to apply it yourself for now — just know that those extra vowels that look like waste have a job; they aren't decoration.

blocks.text: Rule 6 — An extra letter in front of a word covers the original (urú)

The second change is called **urú** (OO-roo, literally "eclipsis"). A new letter is written **in front of** the original one, and the original stops being pronounced — just like the moon covering the sun. You only read the letter in front.

Only those seven letters are eclipsed (b, c, d, f, g, p, t). A word starting with a vowel gets **n-** in front: *ár n-athair* ("our father"). When séimhiú is used and when urú is used is the subject of all of Unit 19; until then, every time one appears it's flagged in the unit notes.

blocks.title: If a word isn't in the dictionary, take its hat off first
items: Dictionaries list words in their bare form. *Bhean* isn't in the dictionary — look up *bean*. *Gcarr* isn't there — look up *carr*. *Dteach* isn't there — look up *teach*.
Quick method: if the second letter is **h**, drop the h. If the first two letters are one of the urú pairs in the table above, drop the first letter.
The only tricky one is *bhf-*: drop **two** letters, leaving *f-*. *Bhfuil* → *fuil*, from the verb *bí*.

blocks.title: Five words to practice everything at once
items: *Gaeilge* → GAYL-guh — "the Irish language". Notice *ae* becomes "ay", and the second *g* is slender because it sits between e's.
*Sláinte* → SLAWN-tyuh — "health". The fada lengthens the a; the *te* at the end is slender, so it's "tyeh".
*Oíche mhaith* → EE-khuh WAH — "good night". Broad *mh* becomes w; the *th* at the end almost disappears.
*Go raibh maith agat* → guh ROV MAH AH-gut — "thank you". Four words, read as one, and this is the sentence you'll say most often in Ireland.

*Dia duit* → DYEE-uh DWIT — "hello", literally "God to-you". In native speakers' mouths the second word almost always sounds like *dhuit* (DYEE-uh GHWIT), and some writers spell it that way; if you can't make the *gh* sound yet, "DYEE-uh WIT" is understood everywhere.

blocks.text: Everything from the twenty units, packed into ten tables. This chapter is for coming back to, not for memorizing now.
1. The verb *bí* — "to be (somewhere, in a state)"
The past negative uses a special form, *raibh*: *ní raibh mé*, *an raibh tú?* Future negative: *ní bheidh mé*, *an mbeidh tú?*
2. The copula *is* (an chopail) — for saying who or what something is

blocks.title: When *tá* and when *is*
items: *Tá* for states, places, and things that can change: *Tá mé tuirseach* (I'm tired), *Tá mé sa bhaile* (I'm at home).
*Is* for identity and permanent categories: *Is Indinéisigh mé* (I'm Indonesian), *Is dochtúir í* (she's a doctor).
So "I'm a teacher" uses *is*, but "I'm at school" uses *tá*. It's the same split as *ser* and *estar* in Spanish — two verbs where English has one "to be".

blocks.text: 3. Prepositions that swallow pronouns
The three most common uses: **ag** for possession (*Tá carr agam* — I have a car), **ar** for feelings and physical states (*Tá ocras orm* — I'm hungry), **le** for likes (*Is maith liom* — I like).

blocks.text: The first column is the base form — the command form, and the form dictionaries use. The third column is the present-tense "I" form. The fourth column is the verbal noun, used after *ag* to say "…ing". The eleven irregular verbs are marked with an asterisk.

blocks.title: How to use this list
items: Group 2 verbs can be spotted by the ending of the base form: *-igh* (*ceannaigh*, *éirigh*, *tosaigh*) or two syllables ending in *-ir/-il/-is* (*oscail*, *freagair*, *inis*). The rest are group 1.
For other persons, just change the ending of the "I" form in the third column: *ólaim* → *ólann tú*, *ceannaím* → *ceannaíonn sé*.

The fourth column is the form you'll use most in everyday conversation, because Irish prefers *Tá mé ag ól tae* to *Ólaim tae* — much like English prefers "I'm drinking tea" to "I drink tea" for right now.

blocks.text: After twenty units, you'll start spotting the language in unexpected places. This chapter is a small collection.
Signs you'll see in Ireland
Place names — almost all of them short sentences

These three words come up most often and are the most useful to recognize: **baile** (town, giving Bally-), **cill** (church, giving Kil-), and **dún** (fort, giving Dun-/-doon). If you see an Irish town name starting with one of those three, you already know half its meaning.

blocks.title: That first proverb isn't just politeness
items: *Is fearr Gaeilge bhriste ná Béarla cliste* is the sentence Irish people say most often to beginners who apologize for their messy Irish.
Every Irish speaker also speaks English, so nobody *has* to talk to you in Gaeilge. If you try, it's a choice — and it's almost always warmly welcomed.
The most useful sentence to start with: *Tá mé ag foghlaim Gaeilge* — "I'm learning Irish".

blocks.text: These twenty units take you to the end of level A1: you can introduce yourself, ask and answer about family, where you live, work, time, food, and shopping; you can use the three basic tenses; and you can read signs and short sentences without a dictionary. What isn't here yet and is waiting at the next level: the *modh coinníollach* (conditional), the *saorbhriathar* (the subjectless "autonomous" form), the genitive case in full, comparative adjectives, and clauses with *go* and *nach*.
What you can do starting tomorrow

items: **Listen ten minutes a day.** *RTÉ Raidió na Gaeltachta* and the TV channel *TG4* stream free online, and TG4 offers Irish subtitles for most of its programs. Don't try to understand; let the rhythm sink in first.

**Use the right dictionary.** *teanglann.ie* has both the Ó Dónaill and De Bhaldraithe dictionaries, with recordings of every word in three dialects and tables of its forms. *focloir.ie* is lighter for the English→Irish direction.
**Check your writing.** *An Gramadóir* and the checker at *abair.ie* catch the most common séimhiú and urú mistakes — two things you won't notice on your own.
**Find people.** *Pop-Up Gaeltacht* is a relaxed Irish-language meetup now held in dozens of cities around the world, and a *Ciorcal Comhrá* (conversation circle) is almost always open to beginners.
**Read something short.** *Séideán Sí* and the *Gafa* series are written for young readers and fit early A2 nicely. For news in easier language, there's *Tuairisc.ie*.

blocks.title: One last piece of advice about dialects
items: This course uses the standard spelling (*An Caighdeán Oifigiúil*) with Connacht pronunciation. Once you start listening to native speakers, you'll find three different sound regions — Munster in the south, Connacht in the middle, Ulster in the north.
Pick one and stay there for your first year. Switching between dialects early on is the fastest way to end up with a pronunciation nobody recognizes anywhere.
The spelling is the same in all three regions, so whichever you choose, everything in this course still applies.

blocks.text: *Go n-éirí an bóthar leat* — may your road rise with you (may your journey go well). And remember the proverb: *Beatha teanga í a labhairt* — a language lives by being spoken.
